claim: Dopamine type 1 receptors (Drd1) are expressed in unipolar brush cells (UBCs) of the mouse cerebellar vermis.
source: We show that dopamine type 1 receptors (Drd1) are expressed in unipolar brush cells (UBCs) of the mouse cerebellar vermis.
evidence: Supported by fluorescent in situ hybridization data showing Drd1a transcripts in tdT+ UBCs (Figure 1F) and immunohistochemistry showing tdT+ cells with UBC morphology (Figure 1B-C).

claim: Drd1 activation increases UBC firing rate.
source: Drd1 activation increases UBC firing rate and post-synaptic NMDAR -mediated currents.
evidence: Demonstrated by current clamp recordings showing 2.48 Hz increase in firing rate (110% increase from baseline) after SKF81297 application (Figure 2C-D).

claim: Drd1 activation increases post-synaptic NMDAR-mediated currents in UBCs.
source: Drd1 activation increases UBC firing rate and post-synaptic NMDAR -mediated currents.
evidence: Supported by voltage clamp recordings showing 15% increase in peak NMDAR current after SKF81297 application (Figure 2I-K) and glutamate uncaging experiments showing 51% increase in NMDAR current amplitude (Figure 2N-O).

claim: Midbrain dopaminergic nuclei are not the source of cerebellar dopamine.
source: We exclude midbrain dopaminergic nuclei and tyrosine hydroxylase-positive Purkinje (Pkj) cells as potential sources, supporting the possibility of dopaminergic co-release from locus coeruleus (LC) axons.
evidence: Supported by retrograde tracing showing no labeling in SNc/VTA (Figure 3A-C) and absence of GFP labeling in VTA/SNc neurons in Th-Flpo retrograde experiments (Figure 3G).

claim: Tyrosine hydroxylase-positive Purkinje cells are not the source of cerebellar dopamine.
source: We exclude midbrain dopaminergic nuclei and tyrosine hydroxylase-positive Purkinje (Pkj) cells as potential sources, supporting the possibility of dopaminergic co-release from locus coeruleus (LC) axons.
evidence: Supported by FISH data showing TH+ Pkj cells lack transcripts for Ddc, Slc18a2, and Slc6a3 (Figure 3D-F), which are necessary for dopamine synthesis and release.

claim: Locus coeruleus (LC) axons are a potential source of dopaminergic co-release onto UBCs.
source: We exclude midbrain dopaminergic nuclei and tyrosine hydroxylase-positive Purkinje (Pkj) cells as potential sources, supporting the possibility of dopaminergic co-release from locus coeruleus (LC) axons.
evidence: Supported by retrograde tracing showing GFP+ LC neurons (Figure 3G), rabies virus tracing showing LC inputs to UBCs (Figure 4), and GRABDA2h sensor responses to LC fiber stimulation (Figure 5).

claim: Electrical stimulation of cerebellar inputs elicits monoamine release onto Drd1-expressing UBCs.
source: Using an optical dopamine sensor GRABDA2h, electrical stimulation, and optogenetic activation of LC fibers in the acute slice, we find evidence for monoamine release onto Drd1-expressing UBCs.
evidence: Demonstrated by GRABDA2h fluorescence increases in response to electrical stimulation (50 stimuli, 50 Hz) that were blocked by Drd2 antagonist (Figure 5C-D).

claim: Optogenetic activation of LC fibers elicits monoamine release onto Drd1-expressing UBCs.
source: Using an optical dopamine sensor GRABDA2h, electrical stimulation, and optogenetic activation of LC fibers in the acute slice, we find evidence for monoamine release onto Drd1-expressing UBCs.
evidence: Demonstrated by time-locked increases in GRABDA2h fluorescence in UBCs in response to optical stimulation of LC axons (200 pulses, 39 Hz) in 5/20 cells (Figure 5G-H).

claim: Purkinje cells directly inhibit Drd1-positive UBCs.
source: Pkj cells directly inhibit these Drd1-positive UBCs, forming a dopamine-sensitive recurrent vestibulo-cerebellar circuit.
evidence: Demonstrated by voltage clamp recordings showing short latency IPSCs in 11/24 UBCs in response to optogenetic activation of Pkj cells (Figure 7D-E), which were abolished by gabazine (Figure 7F-H).

claim: Drd1-positive UBCs and Purkinje cells form a dopamine-sensitive recurrent vestibulo-cerebellar circuit.
source: Pkj cells directly inhibit these Drd1-positive UBCs, forming a dopamine-sensitive recurrent vestibulo-cerebellar circuit.
evidence: Supported by data showing Pkj cells inhibit UBCs (Figure 7) and UBCs can alter Pkj cell firing (Figure 6), combined with evidence that UBCs express Drd1 receptors (Figure 1) and receive LC inputs (Figures 3-5).

claim: All tdT+ cells in the cerebellum of Drd1-Cre;tdTomato mice are positive for Eomesodermin (Tbr2), a known marker for UBCs.
source: All tdT+ cells in the cerebellum were positive for nuclear protein Eomesodermin (Tbr2), a known marker for UBCs (Englund et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging showing 100% overlap of tdT+ cells with Tbr2 (Figure 1C) and citation to prior literature establishing Tbr2 as a UBC marker.

claim: Only 35% of Tbr2+ UBCs express tdTomato in Drd1-Cre;tdTomato mice.
source: However, only 35% of Tbr2+ UBCs expressed tdT, suggesting that a subpopulation of UBCs expresses tdT driven by Drd1 promoter activity (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Quantified from confocal images showing 178/510 Tbr2+ cells express tdT (Figure 1C).

claim: 71% of tdT+ UBCs express metabotropic glutamate receptor type 1 (mGluR1).
source: The majority of tdT+ neurons expressed metabotropic glutamate receptor type 1 (mGluR1) (Figure 1D) (71%, n = 2 mice, 779 cells).
evidence: Quantified from immunohistochemistry showing 401/779 tdT+ cells express mGluR1 (Figure 1D).

claim: 5.3% of tdT+ UBCs express calretinin (CR).
source: Very few tdT+ UBCs belonged to calretinin+ (CR) type: 5.3% of tdT+ UBCs expressed CR, and 12.5% of CR+ UBCs expressed tdT (Figure 1E).
evidence: Quantified from immunohistochemistry showing 48/1235 tdT+ cells express CR (Figure 1E).

claim: 76% of tdT+ UBCs express Drd1a mRNA transcripts.
source: We found that 76% of tdT+ (Figure 1F) UBCs expressed Drd1a transcripts in low abundance (n = 4 animals, 2553 cells) across an age range from P20s to P60s (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, C).
evidence: Quantified from fluorescent in situ hybridization showing Drd1a transcripts in tdT+ UBCs (Figure 1F).

claim: The density of Drd1a puncta is 40-fold enriched in the volume of tdT+ UBC cell bodies compared with regions outside the cell bodies.
source: The density of Drd1a puncta was 40-fold enriched in the volume of tdT+ ROIs, compared with regions outside the cell bodies (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Quantified from 3D analysis of FISH images showing enrichment of Drd1a puncta within tdT+ soma (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).

claim: Puff application of Drd1 agonist SKF81297 increased the firing rate of tdT+ UBCs by 2.48 Hz (110% increase from baseline).
source: Puff application of selective Drd1 agonist SKF81297 increased the firing rate of tdT+ UBCs over a period of 10 min (Figure 2C–D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) (2.48 Hz increase, 110% increase from baseline, n = 13 cells, paired Wilcoxon signed rank test, p=0.02).
evidence: Measured from current clamp recordings comparing baseline and SKF81297 application periods (Figure 2C-D).

claim: Application of SKF81297 in the presence of Drd1 antagonists does not significantly change UBC firing rate.
source: We recorded two separate control datasets, one where we applied SKF81297 in the presence of a Drd1 antagonist cocktail (SKF83566, SCH39166, and SCH23390; n = 13 cells, paired Wilcoxon signed rank test, p=0.49), and an independent dataset where we delivered puff application of artificial cerebrospinal fluid (ACSF; n = 13 cells, paired Wilcoxon signed rank test, p=0.33) (Figure 2E, F).
evidence: Measured from current clamp recordings showing no significant change in firing rate with antagonist present (Figure 2E-F).

claim: Puff application of ACSF does not significantly change UBC firing rate.
source: We recorded two separate control datasets, one where we applied SKF81297 in the presence of a Drd1 antagonist cocktail (SKF83566, SCH39166, and SCH23390; n = 13 cells, paired Wilcoxon signed rank test, p=0.49), and an independent dataset where we delivered puff application of artificial cerebrospinal fluid (ACSF; n = 13 cells, paired Wilcoxon signed rank test, p=0.33) (Figure 2E, F).
evidence: Measured from current clamp recordings showing no significant change in firing rate with ACSF application (Figure 2E-F).

claim: Drd1 activation increases resting membrane potential in UBCs.
source: Increases in firing rate, membrane potential, and relative input resistance were detected in response to Drd1 activation, but absent in both control groups (Figure 2E, F).
evidence: Measured from current clamp recordings comparing baseline and SKF81297 application periods (Figure 2E-F).

claim: Drd1 activation increases relative input resistance in UBCs.
source: Increases in firing rate, membrane potential, and relative input resistance were detected in response to Drd1 activation, but absent in both control groups (Figure 2E, F).
evidence: Measured from current clamp recordings comparing baseline and SKF81297 application periods (Figure 2E-F).

claim: Application of 10 µM SKF81297 increases peak amplitude of NMDAR currents in UBCs by 15%.
source: Using electrical stimulation of mossy fibers, we found an increase in peak amplitude of NMDAR currents after the flow in of 10 µM SKF81297 (Figure 2I–K) (15% increase in peak current, n = 9 cells, paired t-test, p=0.0251).
evidence: Measured from voltage clamp recordings with electrical stimulation of mossy fibers (Figure 2I-K).

claim: Glutamate uncaging-evoked NMDAR currents in UBCs increase by 51% in the presence of 10 µM SKF81297.
source: NMDAR-mediated currents in response to 1-ms long pulses of 725 nm laser light were compared for experiments with and without 10 µM SKF81297 present in the bath. Current amplitudes increased with Drd1 activation, consistent with a post-synaptic mechanism of action (Figure 2N–O) (51% increase of average amplitude, n = 13 cells, unpaired t-test, p=0.0068).
evidence: Measured from two-photon glutamate uncaging experiments comparing ACSF and SKF81297 conditions (Figure 2N-O).

claim: The increase in NMDAR currents with Drd1 activation is mediated by a post-synaptic mechanism.
source: Current amplitudes increased with Drd1 activation, consistent with a post-synaptic mechanism of action (Figure 2N–O) (51% increase of average amplitude, n = 13 cells, unpaired t-test, p=0.0068).
evidence: Demonstrated by glutamate uncaging experiments that bypass presynaptic terminals showing increased NMDAR currents with SKF81297 (Figure 2N-O).

claim: No retrograde labeling of Dat-Cre;tdT neurons in the SNc/VTA was observed after CTB-488 injection into lobules IX/X of the cerebellum.
source: First, to evaluate whether Drd1+ UBCs could receive inputs from midbrain dopamine neurons, we carried out retrograde tracing from lobules IX/X of the vestibulo-cerebellum in a Dat-Cre;tdT mouse cross. We found no support for the existence of this projection (Figure 3A–C), despite the abundance of Dat-Cre;tdT axonal fibers in the cerebellum (Figure 3B, inset).
evidence: Demonstrated by retrograde tracing experiments showing no CTB-488 labeling in VTA/SNc tdT+ neurons (Figure 3B-C).

claim: Retrograde labeling from the cerebellum labels tdT+ neurons in the lateral reticular nucleus (LRN) in Dat-Cre;tdT mice.
source: Retrograde labeling confirmed that these tdT+ axons originate from a pre-cerebellar brainstem nucleus, the lateral reticular nucleus (LRN), and not the SNc/VTA.
evidence: Demonstrated by retrograde CTB-488 injection showing labeling in LRN but not VTA/SNc (Figure 3C).

claim: LRN neurons are glutamatergic and form mossy fiber rosettes within the cerebellum.
source: LRN neurons are glutamatergic, forming mossy fiber rosettes within the cerebellum (Rajakumar et al., 1992; Wu et al., 1999).
evidence: Cited from prior literature (Rajakumar et al., 1992; Wu et al., 1999).

claim: Few LRN neurons express mRNA for tyrosine hydroxylase (Th) or vesicular monoamine transporter type 2 (Slc18a2/Vmat2).
source: To evaluate the expression of transcripts required for dopamine release, we carried out FISH labeling in the LRN and found that few neurons express mRNA for either TH or vesicular monoamine transporter type 2 (Slc18a2/Vmat2) (n = 3 mice, Th,19/135 LRN cells, Slc18a2 2/135 LRN cells) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B-D).
evidence: Quantified from FISH showing 19/135 LRN cells express Th and 2/135 express Slc18a2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B-D).

claim: TH+ Purkinje cells in lobule X lack transcripts for dopa decarboxylase (Ddc).
source: Despite the presence of Th, these neurons lacked the transcripts for dopa decarboxylase (Ddc), the enzyme responsible for converting L-DOPA to dopamine (Figure 3E–F) (n = 2 mice, 163 cells).
evidence: Demonstrated by FISH showing 8/163 TH+ Pkj cells express Ddc compared to 119/134 SNc neurons (Figure 3E-F).

claim: TH+ Purkinje cells in lobule X have minimal expression of Slc18a2 (vesicular monoamine transporter type 2).
source: Similarly, we found minimal expression of Slc18a2 or dopamine active transporter (Slc6a3/Dat), in contrast to Th+ neurons of the SNc (Figure 3D and F).
evidence: Demonstrated by FISH showing 4/37 TH+ Pkj cells express Slc18a2 compared to 102/110 SNc neurons (Figure 3F).

claim: TH+ Purkinje cells in lobule X have minimal expression of Slc6a3 (dopamine active transporter/DAT).
source: Similarly, we found minimal expression of Slc18a2 or dopamine active transporter (Slc6a3/Dat), in contrast to Th+ neurons of the SNc (Figure 3D and F).
evidence: Demonstrated by FISH showing 4/37 TH+ Pkj cells express Slc6a3 compared to 94/110 SNc neurons (Figure 3F).

claim: Locus coeruleus neurons project to lobules IX/X of the cerebellum.
source: To verify that the LC projects specifically to cerebellar regions enriched in Drd1+ UBCs, we used a Th-Flpo mouse line. We injected a retrograde adeno-associated virus (AAV2/retro-CAG-fDIO-Cre-EGFP) into lobules IX/X and found green fluorescent protein+ (GFP) LC neurons (Figure 3G).
evidence: Demonstrated by retrograde AAV injection showing GFP+ LC neurons (Figure 3G).

claim: SNc and VTA do not project to lobules IX/X of the cerebellum.
source: The SNc and VTA did not express GFP, further confirming the absence of a TH+ projection from VTA/SNc.
evidence: Demonstrated by retrograde AAV injection showing no GFP labeling in SNc/VTA (Figure 3G).

claim: Drd1+ UBCs receive pre-synaptic inputs from Purkinje cells.
source: Our data (n = 4 mice, starter cells 33.5 ± 3.9 /mouse) show pre-synaptic labeling of Pkj cells, Golgi cells, cerebellar nuclei neurons, vestibular nuclei neurons, and a sparse population of LC neurons (Figure 4B–E).
evidence: Demonstrated by trans-synaptic rabies virus tracing showing tdT-labeled Pkj cells (Figure 4B-E).

claim: Drd1+ UBCs receive pre-synaptic inputs from Golgi cells.
source: Our data (n = 4 mice, starter cells 33.5 ± 3.9 /mouse) show pre-synaptic labeling of Pkj cells, Golgi cells, cerebellar nuclei neurons, vestibular nuclei neurons, and a sparse population of LC neurons (Figure 4B–E).
evidence: Demonstrated by trans-synaptic rabies virus tracing showing tdT-labeled Golgi cells (Figure 4B-E).

claim: Drd1+ UBCs receive pre-synaptic inputs from cerebellar nuclei neurons.
source: Our data (n = 4 mice, starter cells 33.5 ± 3.9 /mouse) show pre-synaptic labeling of Pkj cells, Golgi cells, cerebellar nuclei neurons, vestibular nuclei neurons, and a sparse population of LC neurons (Figure 4B–E).
evidence: Demonstrated by trans-synaptic rabies virus tracing showing tdT-labeled cerebellar nuclei neurons (Figure 4B-E).

claim: Drd1+ UBCs receive pre-synaptic inputs from vestibular nuclei neurons.
source: Our data (n = 4 mice, starter cells 33.5 ± 3.9 /mouse) show pre-synaptic labeling of Pkj cells, Golgi cells, cerebellar nuclei neurons, vestibular nuclei neurons, and a sparse population of LC neurons (Figure 4B–E).
evidence: Demonstrated by trans-synaptic rabies virus tracing showing tdT-labeled vestibular nuclei neurons (Figure 4B-E).

claim: Drd1+ UBCs receive pre-synaptic inputs from locus coeruleus neurons.
source: Our data (n = 4 mice, starter cells 33.5 ± 3.9 /mouse) show pre-synaptic labeling of Pkj cells, Golgi cells, cerebellar nuclei neurons, vestibular nuclei neurons, and a sparse population of LC neurons (Figure 4B–E).
evidence: Demonstrated by trans-synaptic rabies virus tracing showing tdT-labeled LC neurons (Figure 4B-E).

claim: No labeling in midbrain dopaminergic nuclei was found in rabies virus tracing from Drd1+ UBCs.
source: We did not find any labeling in the midbrain dopaminergic nuclei, even though input tracing using pseudo-typed rabies viral vectors has been used to label monoaminergic inputs (Schwarz et al., 2015; Wall et al., 2013).
evidence: Reported as absence of labeling in rabies virus tracing experiments (Figure 4).

claim: The majority of inputs to Drd1+ UBCs are from nearby cerebellar nuclei cells.
source: The majority of observed inputs was from nearby cerebellar nuclei cells, consistent with prior reports on their projections back to cerebellar cortex (Houck and Person, 2015; Judd et al., 2021).
evidence: Quantified from rabies virus tracing data (Figure 4D-E) and supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Electrical stimulation of cerebellar cortical inputs (50 stimuli, 50 Hz) elicits an increase in GRABDA2h fluorescence in UBCs.
source: We found that electrical stimulation of inputs to lobule X (50 stimuli, 50 Hz) elicited an increase in GRABDA2h fluorescence in UBCs (Figure 5C).
evidence: Measured from two-photon imaging of GRABDA2h sensor in UBCs during electrical stimulation (Figure 5C).

claim: The increase in GRABDA2h fluorescence in response to electrical stimulation is blocked by Drd2 antagonist L-741,626.
source: This increase could be blocked by bath application of Drd2 antagonist, as expected for this sensor (Figure 5D) (1 µM L-741,626, n = 10 cells, 4.88-fold reduction in peak amplitude, paired t-test, p=0.002).
evidence: Measured from two-photon imaging showing 4.88-fold reduction in GRABDA2h response with L-741,626 (Figure 5D).

claim: LC axons spread broadly across all layers of the cerebellum.
source: Anterograde labeling of axons from the LC to the cerebellum. Left: Injection of AAV1-FLEX-FRT-ChR2-mCherry into the LC shows axons spreading broadly across all layers of the cerebellum (n = 2 mice).
evidence: Demonstrated by anterograde viral tracing showing mCherry+ axons throughout cerebellar layers (Figure 5F).

claim: Optogenetic activation of LC axons (200 pulses, 39 Hz) elicits time-locked increases in GRABDA2h fluorescence in a subset of UBCs (5/20 cells).
source: We imaged GRABDA2h fluorescence in UBCs in the acute slice while optogenetically activating LC axons (200 pulses, 39 Hz, 2 ms pulses, 460 nm). In each experiment, the absence of TH+ Pkj cell labeling was confirmed to ensure selective LC targeting without overflow of ChR2 expression into the cerebellum. We found time-locked increases of GRABDA2h fluorescence in UBCs in response to optical stimulation in a subset of UBCs (n = 2 mice, 5/20 cells) (Figure 5G–H).
evidence: Measured from two-photon imaging of GRABDA2h during optogenetic LC stimulation (Figure 5G-H).

claim: Optically evoked GRABDA2h transients in UBCs have an average success rate of ~40% across responding cells.
source: Optically evoked GRABDA2h transients had an average success rate of ~40% across responding cells.
evidence: Calculated from imaging data of optogenetic LC stimulation experiments (Figure 5G-H).

claim: Bath application of Drd1 agonist SKF81297 (10 µM) increases firing rate in cell-attached recordings of Drd1+ UBCs.
source: First, we performed cell-attached recordings of Drd1+ UBCs, collected data during a baseline period, and then applied 10 µm SKF81297 (Figure 5I). Consistent with our whole-cell current clamp recordings, we measured an increase in spontaneous firing rate in tdT+ UBCs in response to Drd1 agonist (Figure 5J) (n = 10 cells, paired Wilcoxon signed rank test, p=0.002).
evidence: Measured from cell-attached recordings comparing baseline and SKF81297 periods (Figure 5I-J).

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of LC fibers (20 Hz) increases firing rate of Drd1+ UBCs by 1.2 Hz (26% above baseline) in cell-attached recordings.
source: We measured a small but significant increase in the firing rate of Drd1+ UBCs in response to LC fiber stimulation (Figure 5L–M) (1.2 Hz increase, 26% above baseline, n = 8 cells, paired Wilcoxon signed rank test, p=0.02).
evidence: Measured from cell-attached recordings during optogenetic LC stimulation with adrenergic and glutamatergic receptors blocked (Figure 5L-M).

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of LC fibers does not significantly change UBC firing rate in the presence of Drd1 antagonist.
source: In a separate set of experiments with Drd1 antagonist (5 µM SCH39166) present in the bath, we measured no statistically significant changes in firing rate.
evidence: Measured from cell-attached recordings during optogenetic LC stimulation with Drd1 antagonist present (Figure 5L-M).

claim: Optogenetic activation of Drd1+ UBCs causes ChR2+ UBCs to respond with 2-5 action potentials per pulse.
source: We stimulated UBCs with a train of LED pulses (460 nm, 10 Hz, 50 pulses, 1 ms pulse width). Each pulse caused a small burst of action potentials (2–5 APs).
evidence: Measured from cell-attached recordings of ChR2+ UBCs during optogenetic stimulation (Figure 6B-C).

claim: UBCs are more likely to respond with multiple spikes to a pulse at the beginning of a train than at the end.
source: UBCs were more likely to respond with multiple spikes to a pulse at the beginning of the train than at the end (Figure 6B–C).
evidence: Measured from cell-attached recordings showing decreased spike number across pulse train (Figure 6C).

claim: Optogenetic activation of Drd1+ UBCs does not significantly alter average Purkinje cell firing rate.
source: Pkj cells did not significantly alter their average firing rate on trials with optogenetic stimulation (Figure 6D).
evidence: Measured from cell-attached recordings of Pkj cells during UBC optogenetic stimulation (Figure 6D).

claim: In a subset of Purkinje cells, optogenetic stimulation of UBCs causes a brief pause in firing during the 500 ms period after stimulus onset.
source: However, in a subset of Pkj cells, stimulation caused a brief pause in firing during the 500 ms period after the beginning of the optogenetic stimulus (Figure 6E).
evidence: Measured from cell-attached recordings showing decreased firing rate in subset of Pkj cells (Figure 6E-G).

claim: Approximately 28% of Purkinje cells (8/28) are 'Pausers' in response to UBC optogenetic activation.
source: The majority of Pkj cells (18/28) did not significantly alter their firing rate, ~ 28% of cells were 'Pausers' (8/28) and 7% of Pkj cells qualified as 'Bursters' (2/28) (Figure 6F–G).
evidence: Quantified from cell-attached recordings of Pkj cells during UBC optogenetic stimulation (Figure 6F-G).

claim: Approximately 7% of Purkinje cells (2/28) are 'Bursters' in response to UBC optogenetic activation.
source: The majority of Pkj cells (18/28) did not significantly alter their firing rate, ~ 28% of cells were 'Pausers' (8/28) and 7% of Pkj cells qualified as 'Bursters' (2/28) (Figure 6F–G).
evidence: Quantified from cell-attached recordings of Pkj cells during UBC optogenetic stimulation (Figure 6F-G).

claim: Purkinje cells with lower EPSC/IPSC ratios are more likely to pause after UBC activation.
source: We calculated the EPSC/IPSCs charge ratio and plotted it against change in firing rate z-score (Figure 6I). Neurons with lower EPSC/IPSC ratios were more likely to pause after the onset of stimulation, suggesting that in these cells the relatively larger inhibitory current favored the pause.
evidence: Demonstrated by correlation analysis showing R2=0.63 between EPSC/IPSC ratio and firing rate z-score (Figure 6I).

claim: 11 out of 24 UBCs (46%) receive short latency synaptic input from Purkinje cells.
source: In UBC voltage clamp experiments, we found that 11/24 UBCs received short latency synaptic input from Pkj cells (Figure 7D).
evidence: Quantified from voltage clamp recordings of UBCs during optogenetic Pkj cell stimulation (Figure 7D).

claim: UBCs receiving IPSCs from Purkinje cells have a per trial success ratio of 0.64 on average.
source: Cells with successful evoked IPSCs had a per trial success ratio of 0.64 on average (Figure 7D).
evidence: Calculated from voltage clamp recordings showing successful IPSC responses (Figure 7D).

claim: Optically evoked IPSCs in UBCs from Purkinje cells have an average amplitude of 91 pA ± 24.
source: There was significant variability in the amplitude (91 pA, ± 24) (Figure 7H) and timing (9.4 ms ±2.4) (Figure 7E) of optically evoked IPSCs, with some cells exhibiting large currents over the entire stimulation period and others responding with a single large IPSC at the onset of stimulation.
evidence: Measured from voltage clamp recordings of UBCs during optogenetic Pkj cell stimulation (Figure 7H).

claim: Optically evoked IPSCs in UBCs from Purkinje cells have an average latency of 9.4 ms ± 2.4.
source: There was significant variability in the amplitude (91 pA, ± 24) (Figure 7H) and timing (9.4 ms ±2.4) (Figure 7E) of optically evoked IPSCs, with some cells exhibiting large currents over the entire stimulation period and others responding with a single large IPSC at the onset of stimulation.
evidence: Measured from voltage clamp recordings showing time to first IPSC (Figure 7E).

claim: Application of gabazine (10 µM) abolishes evoked IPSCs in UBCs from Purkinje cell stimulation.
source: In a subset of UBCs (n = 9 cells) (Figure 7F–G), we flowed in 10 µM gabazine to ensure the measured currents were due to GABAA channel opening. Application of gabazine abolished all evoked currents (Figure 7H).
evidence: Measured from voltage clamp recordings showing elimination of IPSCs with gabazine (Figure 7F-H).

claim: Cerebellar activity plays a critical function in fine motor learning.
source: Cerebellar activity plays a critical function in fine motor learning (Kalmbach et al., 2010; Raymond and Lisberger, 1998; Woodruff-pak, 1993).
evidence: Cited from prior literature (Kalmbach et al., 2010; Raymond and Lisberger, 1998; Woodruff-pak, 1993).

claim: Important anatomical, molecular, and functional differences between cerebellar lobules are beginning to emerge.
source: The cerebellum is defined by its clearly organized cytoarchitecture; however, important anatomical, molecular, and functional differences between lobules are beginning to emerge.
evidence: General statement about emerging research trends in cerebellar neuroscience.

claim: Unipolar brush cells (UBCs) are glutamatergic interneurons enriched in the granular layer of vestibulo-cerebellum.
source: One key difference between cerebellar lobules is the distribution of unipolar brush cells (UBCs), glutamatergic interneurons enriched in the granular layer of vestibulo-cerebellum, which is known to be involved in processing vestibular sensory input (Mugnaini and Floris, 1994).
evidence: Cited from prior literature (Mugnaini and Floris, 1994).

claim: Vestibulo-cerebellum is involved in processing vestibular sensory input.
source: One key difference between cerebellar lobules is the distribution of unipolar brush cells (UBCs), glutamatergic interneurons enriched in the granular layer of vestibulo-cerebellum, which is known to be involved in processing vestibular sensory input (Mugnaini and Floris, 1994).
evidence: Cited from prior literature (Mugnaini and Floris, 1994).

claim: UBCs reside in the granular layer and receive inputs from mossy fibers.
source: UBCs reside in the granular layer and receive inputs from mossy fibers.
evidence: Established anatomical knowledge about UBC connectivity.

claim: Each UBC axon diverges, releasing glutamate onto multiple local granule cells or other UBCs.
source: Each UBC axon diverges, releasing glutamate onto multiple local granule cells or other UBCs.
evidence: Established anatomical knowledge about UBC connectivity.

claim: UBCs are recurrently connected.
source: Since UBCs are recurrently connected, they are poised to amplify and temporally extend the influence of excitatory inputs into the cerebellum (Requarth and Sawtell, 2014).
evidence: Cited from prior literature (Requarth and Sawtell, 2014).

claim: UBCs are poised to amplify and temporally extend the influence of excitatory inputs into the cerebellum.
source: Since UBCs are recurrently connected, they are poised to amplify and temporally extend the influence of excitatory inputs into the cerebellum (Requarth and Sawtell, 2014).
evidence: Cited from prior literature (Requarth and Sawtell, 2014).

claim: UBCs receiving a single mossy fiber input could form a 'labeled line' input to the granular layer, helping distinguish between inputs from semicircular canals and vestibular nuclei.
source: Alternatively, UBCs—receiving a single mossy fiber input—could form a 'labeled line' input to the granular layer, helping distinguish between inputs from semicircular canals and vestibular nuclei (Balmer and Trussell, 2019).
evidence: Cited from prior literature (Balmer and Trussell, 2019).

claim: UBCs were discovered in the late 1970s.
source: The relatively recent discovery of UBCs in the late 1970s (Altman and Bayer, 1977) and characterization in the 1990s (Mugnaini and Floris, 1994), their sparseness in the cerebellum, and the lack of tools to isolate them have limited our understanding of their functional connectivity.
evidence: Cited from prior literature (Altman and Bayer, 1977).

claim: UBCs were characterized in the 1990s.
source: The relatively recent discovery of UBCs in the late 1970s (Altman and Bayer, 1977) and characterization in the 1990s (Mugnaini and Floris, 1994), their sparseness in the cerebellum, and the lack of tools to isolate them have limited our understanding of their functional connectivity.
evidence: Cited from prior literature (Mugnaini and Floris, 1994).

claim: Norepinephrine regulates cerebellar output.
source: While it is clear that norepinephrine (NE) regulates cerebellar output, the mechanistic details of neuromodulatory effects for other amines remain poorly understood (Basile and Dunwiddie, 1984; Carey and Regehr, 2009; Lanore et al., 2019; Lippiello et al., 2015).
evidence: Cited from prior literature (Basile and Dunwiddie, 1984; Carey and Regehr, 2009; Lanore et al., 2019; Lippiello et al., 2015).

claim: Dopamine type 1 receptor (Drd1) is expressed within the granular layer of the cerebellum.
source: Previous reports posit the expression of dopamine type 1 receptor (Drd1) within the granular layer of the cerebellum (Locke et al., 2018; Panagopoulos et al., 1993).
evidence: Cited from prior literature (Locke et al., 2018; Panagopoulos et al., 1993).

claim: Several groups have previously reported dopaminergic projections from the substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc) and the ventral tegmental area (VTA) targeting the cerebellar cortex of rats and monkeys.
source: Additionally, several groups have previously reported dopaminergic projections from the substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc) and the ventral tegmental area (VTA), targeting the cerebellar cortex of rats and monkeys (Melchitzky and Lewis, 2000; Panagopoulos et al., 1991).
evidence: Cited from prior literature (Melchitzky and Lewis, 2000; Panagopoulos et al., 1991).

claim: Recent work in mice did not find evidence for projections from midbrain dopaminergic nuclei to the cerebellum.
source: Yet, recent work in mice did not find evidence for projections from midbrain dopaminergic nuclei to the cerebellum.
evidence: Reference to recent unpublished or published work, context suggests citation but none provided in this sentence.

claim: Vestibulo-cerebellar Purkinje cells express tyrosine hydroxylase (TH), the rate-limiting enzyme in the classical dopamine synthesis pathway.
source: Vestibulo-cerebellar Pkj cells express TH, the rate-limiting enzyme in the classical dopamine (DA) synthesis pathway (Abbott et al., 1996; Huang et al., 2016; Sawada et al., 2004; Takada et al., 1993).
evidence: Cited from prior literature (Abbott et al., 1996; Huang et al., 2016; Sawada et al., 2004; Takada et al., 1993).

claim: Purkinje cells release dopamine onto their own dendrites, which express dopamine type 2 receptor (Drd2).
source: One prior report details a dendritic release of dopamine by Pkj cells onto their own dendrites, expressing dopamine type 2 receptor (Drd2) (Kim et al., 2009).
evidence: Cited from prior literature (Kim et al., 2009).

claim: Locus coeruleus releases dopamine as well as norepinephrine in the hippocampus.
source: A third potential source of cerebellar dopamine is the locus coeruleus (LC), recently demonstrated to release dopamine as well as NE in the hippocampus (Kawahara et al., 2001; Kempadoo et al., 2016; Takeuchi et al., 2016).
evidence: Cited from prior literature (Kawahara et al., 2001; Kempadoo et al., 2016; Takeuchi et al., 2016).

claim: The proposed mechanism for dual amine co-release from locus coeruleus is incomplete conversion of dopamine to norepinephrine in the vesicles.
source: The proposed mechanism of action for this dual amine co-release is incomplete conversion of dopamine to NE in the vesicles.
evidence: Inferred from prior literature on LC dopamine/norepinephrine co-release mechanisms.

claim: tdT+ cells in the cerebellar cortex of Drd1-Cre;tdTomato mice are distributed across the cerebellar granular layer and enriched in lobules IX and X of the cerebellar vermis, lobules VIb and VII, and the paraflocculus.
source: Analysis of Drd1-Cre;tdTomato (tdT) expression in the cerebellar cortex revealed numerous small tdT+ cells distributed across the cerebellar granular layer (Figure 1A), enriched in lobules IX and X of the cerebellar vermis, lobules VIb and VII, and the paraflocculus.
evidence: Observed from whole brain imaging of Drd1-Cre;tdT mice (Figure 1A).

claim: Cerebellar tdT+ cells in Drd1-Cre;tdTomato mice possess the morphological features of UBCs: a single large dendritic brush and a medium-sized soma relative to granule cells.
source: Confocal imaging confirmed that cerebellar tdT+ cells possess the morphological features of UBCs: a single large dendritic brush and a medium-sized soma relative to granule cells (Figure 1B).
evidence: Observed from confocal imaging of tdT+ cells (Figure 1B).

claim: 65% of mGluR1+ UBCs express tdTomato in Drd1-Cre;tdTomato mice.
source: The mGluR1+ and tdT+ populations did not overlap completely, as only 65% of mGluR1+ UBCs expressed tdT.
evidence: Quantified from immunohistochemistry showing 401/779 mGluR1+ cells express tdT (Figure 1D).

claim: 12.5% of calretinin+ (CR) UBCs express tdTomato in Drd1-Cre;tdTomato mice.
source: Very few tdT+ UBCs belonged to calretinin+ (CR) type: 5.3% of tdT+ UBCs expressed CR, and 12.5% of CR+ UBCs expressed tdT (Figure 1E).
evidence: Quantified from immunohistochemistry showing 48/1235 CR+ cells express tdT (Figure 1E).

claim: In the Drd1-Cre;tdT cross, all cerebellar tdT+ cells are UBCs.
source: Given these data, we infer that in the Drd1-Cre;tdT cross, all cerebellar tdT+ cells are UBCs, and that these tdT+ UBCs are a subset of the total UBC population, mostly comprised of mGluR1+ ON UBCs.
evidence: Inferred from data showing all tdT+ cells express Tbr2 (Figure 1C) and have UBC morphology (Figure 1B).

claim: tdT+ UBCs in Drd1-Cre;tdT mice are a subset of the total UBC population, mostly comprised of mGluR1+ ON UBCs.
source: Given these data, we infer that in the Drd1-Cre;tdT cross, all cerebellar tdT+ cells are UBCs, and that these tdT+ UBCs are a subset of the total UBC population, mostly comprised of mGluR1+ ON UBCs.
evidence: Inferred from data showing 35% of Tbr2+ UBCs express tdT (Figure 1C) and 71% of tdT+ cells express mGluR1 (Figure 1D).

claim: A prior report using a different Drd1-Cre mouse line reported the expression of Drd1 receptors in deep cerebellar nuclei.
source: A prior report using a different Drd1-Cre mouse line reported the expression of Drd1 receptors in deep cerebellar nuclei (Locke et al., 2018).
evidence: Cited from prior literature (Locke et al., 2018).

claim: In the Drd1-Cre;tdTomato cross used in this study, there is no expression of tdT in the cerebellar nuclei.
source: In contrast, we do not see expression of tdT in the cerebellar nuclei in this transgenic cross.
evidence: Observed from imaging of Drd1-Cre;tdT mice showing no tdT expression in cerebellar nuclei.

claim: Cre recombinase lines can show developmentally regulated expression patterns.
source: Because Cre recombinase lines can show developmentally regulated expression patterns, next we evaluated whether tdT+ UBCs contain Drd1 receptors using fluorescent in situ hybridization (FISH) to label tdT and Drd1a mRNA transcripts.
evidence: General knowledge about Cre recombinase line properties.

claim: Most Drd1 UBCs express a low amount of Drd1 transcripts.
source: Most Drd1 UBCs express a low amount of Drd1 transcripts.
evidence: Observed from FISH data showing low abundance of Drd1a transcripts in tdT+ UBCs (Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).

claim: Most tdT+ UBCs (70%) increased their firing rate in response to Drd1 activation.
source: Most tdT+ UBCs (70%) increased their firing rate in response to Drd1 activation, as has been reported for Drd1-mediated effects on striatal spiny projection neurons (Lahiri and Bevan, 2020).
evidence: Calculated from current clamp recordings showing 9/13 cells increased firing rate with SKF81297 (Figure 2C-D).

claim: Drd1-mediated effects increase firing rate in striatal spiny projection neurons.
source: Most tdT+ UBCs (70%) increased their firing rate in response to Drd1 activation, as has been reported for Drd1-mediated effects on striatal spiny projection neurons (Lahiri and Bevan, 2020).
evidence: Cited from prior literature (Lahiri and Bevan, 2020).

claim: Quiescent UBCs characterized by hyperpolarized resting membrane potential did not initiate activity in response to Drd1 agonist.
source: Quiescent neurons characterized by hyperpolarized resting membrane potential did not initiate activity in response to pharmacological stimulus.
evidence: Observed from current clamp recordings showing some cells did not respond to SKF81297 (Figure 2C-D).

claim: Drd1 activation increases NMDAR currents in prefrontal cortex neurons.
source: Prior research shows an increase in N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor (NMDAR) currents during the activation of Drd1 receptors on neurons in the prefrontal cortex (Chen et al., 2004).
evidence: Cited from prior literature (Chen et al., 2004).

claim: The measured NMDAR currents in UBCs were blocked by the application of NMDAR antagonist CPP (10 µM).
source: In a subset of experiments, we verified that the measured currents were blocked by the application of NMDAR antagonist CPP (10 µM, n = 5 cells) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: Demonstrated by voltage clamp recordings showing elimination of currents with CPP (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G).

claim: UBCs are recurrently connected, so the increase in NMDAR currents may be downstream of a post-synaptic mechanism or a consequence of increased excitability in presynaptic UBCs.
source: Since UBCs are recurrently connected, the increase in NMDAR currents may be downstream of a post-synaptic mechanism or a consequence of increased excitability in presynaptic UBCs.
evidence: Logical inference based on known UBC connectivity and experimental observations.

claim: The increase in NMDAR currents with Drd1 activation in UBCs is consistent with a post-synaptic mechanism of action.
source: NMDAR-mediated currents in response to 1-ms long pulses of 725 nm laser light were compared for experiments with and without 10 µM SKF81297 present in the bath. Current amplitudes increased with Drd1 activation, consistent with a post-synaptic mechanism of action (Figure 2N–O) (51% increase of average amplitude, n = 13 cells, unpaired t-test, p=0.0068).
evidence: Demonstrated by glutamate uncaging experiments that bypass presynaptic terminals (Figure 2N-O).

claim: Additional mechanisms beyond NMDAR modulation likely account for observed changes in UBC excitability with Drd1 activation.
source: These experiments support an NMDAR-mediated component to Drd1 activation in UBCs, although given prior findings in the striatum and prefrontal cortex, it is likely that additional mechanisms account for observed changes in excitability (Gorelova and Yang, 2000; Surmeier and Kitai, 1993).
evidence: Inferred from comparison with prior literature (Gorelova and Yang, 2000; Surmeier and Kitai, 1993) and experimental observations.

claim: Dat-Cre;tdT axonal fibers in the cerebellum are morphologically consistent with mossy fiber terminals and are restricted to the granule layer.
source: Retrograde labeling confirmed that these tdT+ axons originate from a pre-cerebellar brainstem nucleus, the lateral reticular nucleus (LRN), and not the SNc/VTA. LRN neurons are glutamatergic, forming mossy fiber rosettes within the cerebellum (Rajakumar et al., 1992; Wu et al., 1999).
evidence: Observed from imaging showing tdT+ fibers with mossy fiber morphology (Figure 3B inset) and confirmed by retrograde tracing to LRN.

claim: There are no prior reports of LRN neurons expressing proteins required for dopamine synthesis or packaging.
source: There are no prior reports of LRN neurons expressing proteins required for dopamine synthesis or packaging.
evidence: Statement about absence of prior literature on this topic.

claim: TH is expressed in Purkinje cells of vermal lobules IX and X.
source: Next, using FISH and antibody labeling, we confirmed previous reports of TH expression in Pkj cells of vermal lobules IX and X (Figure 3D-F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A; Austin et al., 1992; Sakai et al., 1995; Takada et al., 1993).
evidence: Confirmed by FISH and immunohistochemistry (Figure 3D-F) and cited from prior literature (Austin et al., 1992; Sakai et al., 1995; Takada et al., 1993).

claim: Dopamine release from TH+ Purkinje cells is unlikely.
source: Thus, dopamine release from TH+ Pkj cells is unlikely.
evidence: Inferred from FISH data showing TH+ Pkj cells lack Ddc, Slc18a2, and Slc6a3 transcripts (Figure 3D-F).

claim: The most likely source of dopamine to the Drd1+ UBCs is the locus coeruleus.
source: Given these anatomical data, the most likely source of dopamine to the Drd1+ UBCs is the LC.
evidence: Inferred from exclusion of SNc/VTA and TH+ Pkj cells, combined with positive evidence for LC projections (Figure 3).

claim: Trans-synaptic tracing with modified rabies virus CVS-N2cΔG allows labeling of all pre-synaptic partners of neurons expressing Cre recombinase.
source: To assay dopaminergic pre-synaptic inputs to UBCs, we performed trans-synaptic tracing with a modified rabies virus CVS-N2cΔG (Reardon et al., 2016) which allowed us to label all pre-synaptic partners of neurons expressing Cre recombinase (Figure 4A).
evidence: Cited from prior literature (Reardon et al., 2016) describing the rabies virus tracing method.

claim: The modified rabies virus CVS-N2cΔG cannot enter cells that do not express the tumor virus receptor A (TVA).
source: The modified rabies virus construct cannot enter cells that do not express the tumor virus receptor A (TVA); it also lacks the glycoprotein necessary to replicate into mature virus that can travel pre-synaptically.
evidence: Description of the technical properties of the modified rabies virus system.

claim: The modified rabies virus CVS-N2cΔG lacks the glycoprotein necessary to replicate into mature virus that can travel pre-synaptically.
source: The modified rabies virus construct cannot enter cells that do not express the tumor virus receptor A (TVA); it also lacks the glycoprotein necessary to replicate into mature virus that can travel pre-synaptically.
evidence: Description of the technical properties of the modified rabies virus system.

claim: Semicircular canal neurons project directly to mGluR1+ UBCs.
source: We did not dissect semicircular canals or otoliths, so they are not included in this analysis, although previous research shows that semicircular canal neurons project directly to mGluR1+ UBCs (Balmer and Trussell, 2019).
evidence: Cited from prior literature (Balmer and Trussell, 2019).

claim: It is unknown whether rabies virus labels certain pre-synaptic inputs preferentially based on properties such as firing rates, axonal length and structure, or neurotransmitter identity.
source: It is unknown whether the rabies virus labels certain pre-synaptic inputs preferentially based on properties such as firing rates, axonal length and structure, or neurotransmitter identity (Rogers and Beier, 2021).
evidence: Cited from prior literature (Rogers and Beier, 2021) discussing limitations of rabies virus tracing.

claim: Cerebellar nuclei cells project back to cerebellar cortex.
source: The majority of observed inputs was from nearby cerebellar nuclei cells, consistent with prior reports on their projections back to cerebellar cortex (Houck and Person, 2015; Judd et al., 2021).
evidence: Cited from prior literature (Houck and Person, 2015; Judd et al., 2021).

claim: Pseudo-typed rabies viral vectors have been used to label monoaminergic inputs.
source: We did not find any labeling in the midbrain dopaminergic nuclei, even though input tracing using pseudo-typed rabies viral vectors has been used to label monoaminergic inputs (Schwarz et al., 2015; Wall et al., 2013).
evidence: Cited from prior literature (Schwarz et al., 2015; Wall et al., 2013).

claim: GRABDA2h is preferentially activated by dopamine but maintains a slight sensitivity to norepinephrine (dopamine EC50 = 0.13 µM, NE EC50 = 1.7 µM).
source: GRABDA2h is preferentially activated by dopamine, but it maintains a slight sensitivity to NE (dopamine EC50 = 0.13 µM, NE EC50 = 1.7 µM) (Sun et al., 2020).
evidence: Cited from prior literature (Sun et al., 2020) describing GRABDA2h sensor properties.

claim: Drd1 receptors activate Gαs-coupled protein cascades.
source: Since Drd1 receptors activate Gαs-coupled protein cascades (Stoof and Kebabian, 1984; Surmeier and Kitai, 1993), and whole-cell recordings can dialyze cytosolic proteins involved in G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) signaling (Lahiri and Bevan, 2020), we decided to use cell-attached recordings to measure potential effect of dopamine release from LC axons.
evidence: Cited from prior literature (Stoof and Kebabian, 1984; Surmeier and Kitai, 1993).

claim: Whole-cell recordings can dialyze cytosolic proteins involved in G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) signaling.
source: Since Drd1 receptors activate Gαs-coupled protein cascades (Stoof and Kebabian, 1984; Surmeier and Kitai, 1993), and whole-cell recordings can dialyze cytosolic proteins involved in G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) signaling (Lahiri and Bevan, 2020), we decided to use cell-attached recordings to measure potential effect of dopamine release from LC axons.
evidence: Cited from prior literature (Lahiri and Bevan, 2020).

claim: LC neurons have been shown to release glutamate.
source: Additionally, since LC neurons have been shown to release glutamate (Fung et al., 1994; Yang et al., 2021), we blocked AMPA and NMDA receptor mediated excitatory neurotransmission using NBQX (5 µM) and CPP (10 µM).
evidence: Cited from prior literature (Fung et al., 1994; Yang et al., 2021).

claim: The blockade of NMDA receptors would be expected to abolish a fraction of Drd1 activation effects in UBCs.
source: Notably, the blockade of NMDA receptors would be expected to abolish a fraction of Drd1 activation effects (based on our results in Figure 2H–O), providing a strong test of the existence of additional mechanisms altering cellular excitability in UBCs downstream of Drd1 stimulation.
evidence: Inferred from prior experimental results showing NMDAR involvement in Drd1 effects (Figure 2H-O).

claim: GPCR cascades have many downstream targets.
source: GPCR cascades have many downstream targets, and so it is not surprising that several mechanisms could be responsible for changes in firing rate.
evidence: General knowledge about GPCR signaling pathways.

claim: Glutamate can open TRPC3 channels through mGluR1 activation.
source: TRPC3 channels were blocked using Pyr-3 (1 µM) to avoid glutamate opening TRPC3 channels through mGluR1 activation (Sekerková et al., 2013).
evidence: Cited from prior literature (Sekerková et al., 2013).

claim: Purkinje cells express adrenergic receptors.
source: Pkj cells express adrenergic and Drd2 receptors (Basile and Dunwiddie, 1984; Cutando et al., 2019; Kim et al., 2009; Lippiello et al., 2015); to avoid polysynaptic effects from the release of monoamines from LC fibers, we blocked fast inhibitory transmission using gabazine (10 µM) and strychnine (1 µM).
evidence: Cited from prior literature (Basile and Dunwiddie, 1984; Cutando et al., 2019; Kim et al., 2009; Lippiello et al., 2015).

claim: Purkinje cells express Drd2 receptors.
source: Pkj cells express adrenergic and Drd2 receptors (Basile and Dunwiddie, 1984; Cutando et al., 2019; Kim et al., 2009; Lippiello et al., 2015); to avoid polysynaptic effects from the release of monoamines from LC fibers, we blocked fast inhibitory transmission using gabazine (10 µM) and strychnine (1 µM).
evidence: Cited from prior literature (Basile and Dunwiddie, 1984; Cutando et al., 2019; Kim et al., 2009; Lippiello et al., 2015).

claim: Simultaneous activation of Drd1+ UBCs induces a decrease in Purkinje cell firing in a subset of cells.
source: These data demonstrate that simultaneous activation of Drd1+ UBCs induces a decrease in Pkj cell firing.
evidence: Demonstrated by cell-attached recordings showing pausing in subset of Pkj cells during UBC optogenetic activation (Figure 6E-G).

claim: Vestibulo-cerebellar Purkinje cells synapse onto neurons of the cerebellar nuclei.
source: Pkj cells are canonically known to synapse onto neurons of the cerebellar nuclei (Telgkamp et al., 2004), and recent work showed that in the vestibulo-cerebellum Pkj cells make inhibitory connections with nearby granular cells (Guo et al., 2016).
evidence: Cited from prior literature (Telgkamp et al., 2004).

claim: In the vestibulo-cerebellum, Purkinje cells make inhibitory connections with nearby granular cells.
source: Pkj cells are canonically known to synapse onto neurons of the cerebellar nuclei (Telgkamp et al., 2004), and recent work showed that in the vestibulo-cerebellum Pkj cells make inhibitory connections with nearby granular cells (Guo et al., 2016).
evidence: Cited from prior literature (Guo et al., 2016).

claim: Purkinje cell feedback to granule cells appears to be restricted to the vestibular regions of the cerebellar cortex.
source: Notably, Pkj cell feedback to granule cells appears to be restricted to the vestibular regions of the cerebellar cortex, with important implications for the recurrent activity of Pkj cells in these lobules.
evidence: Inferred from prior literature on Pkj-granule cell connectivity.

claim: Purkinje cells directly inhibit mGluR1+ UBCs.
source: These inhibitory connections have also been described in parallel work by another lab (Guo et al., 2021) for mGluR1+ UBCs.
evidence: Cited from parallel work (Guo et al., 2021).

claim: LC neurons are activated in a wide range of behaviors, including deployment of attention, sleep-wake transitions, and locomotion.
source: LC neurons are activated in a wide range of behaviors, including deployment of attention (Aston-Jones et al., 1999), sleep-wake transitions (Hayat et al., 2020), and locomotion (Xiang et al., 2019).
evidence: Cited from prior literature (Aston-Jones et al., 1999; Hayat et al., 2020; Xiang et al., 2019).

claim: There is longstanding evidence of the LC modulating Purkinje cell activity through the release of norepinephrine.
source: There is longstanding evidence of the LC modulating Pkj cell activity through the release of NE (Basile and Dunwiddie, 1984; Lippiello et al., 2015), and recent work shows adrenergic signaling in Golgi cells as well (Lanore et al., 2019).
evidence: Cited from prior literature (Basile and Dunwiddie, 1984; Lippiello et al., 2015).

claim: Recent work shows adrenergic signaling in Golgi cells.
source: There is longstanding evidence of the LC modulating Pkj cell activity through the release of NE (Basile and Dunwiddie, 1984; Lippiello et al., 2015), and recent work shows adrenergic signaling in Golgi cells as well (Lanore et al., 2019).
evidence: Cited from prior literature (Lanore et al., 2019).

claim: The LC could release dopamine onto Drd2 expressing Purkinje cells in addition to UBCs.
source: Our findings suggest that the LC could release dopamine onto other cells in the cerebellum, such as Drd2 expressing Pkj cells (Kim et al., 2009; Mengod et al., 1989), in addition to UBCs.
evidence: Speculated based on current findings and prior literature (Kim et al., 2009; Mengod et al., 1989).

claim: LC neurons respond to rotations of the neck.
source: First, LC neurons respond to rotations of the neck (Manzoni et al., 2009; Pompeiano et al., 1991).
evidence: Cited from prior literature (Manzoni et al., 2009; Pompeiano et al., 1991).

claim: Vestibulo-cerebellar Purkinje cells project to the locus coeruleus as well as the vestibular nuclei.
source: Second, vestibulo-cerebellar Pkj cells project to the LC as well as the vestibular nuclei (Schwarz et al., 2015).
evidence: Cited from prior literature (Schwarz et al., 2015).

claim: Vestibular nuclei make synaptic connections in the cerebellum.
source: Finally, vestibular nuclei make synaptic connections in the cerebellum (Balmer and Trussell, 2019; Päällysaho et al., 1991) and receive projections from the LC (Schuerger and Balaban, 1993).
evidence: Cited from prior literature (Balmer and Trussell, 2019; Päällysaho et al., 1991).

claim: Vestibular nuclei receive projections from the locus coeruleus.
source: Finally, vestibular nuclei make synaptic connections in the cerebellum (Balmer and Trussell, 2019; Päällysaho et al., 1991) and receive projections from the LC (Schuerger and Balaban, 1993).
evidence: Cited from prior literature (Schuerger and Balaban, 1993).

claim: Norepinephrine and dopamine from LC fibers could play a role in vestibular processing.
source: This interconnectivity between the three regions suggests that NE and dopamine from LC fibers could play a role in vestibular processing.
evidence: Speculated based on anatomical connectivity data and current findings.

claim: UBCs have been found in three distinct brain circuits implicated in the cancelation of self-generated cues due to an animal's movement.
source: UBCs have been found in three distinct brain circuits implicated in the cancelation of self-generated cues due to an animal's movement (Requarth and Sawtell, 2014; Singla et al., 2017; Warren and Sawtell, 2016).
evidence: Cited from prior literature (Requarth and Sawtell, 2014; Singla et al., 2017; Warren and Sawtell, 2016).

claim: UBC activity can significantly alter mossy fiber signals to the cerebellum.
source: Their position in the input layer of the cerebellum means that their activity can significantly alter mossy fiber signals to the cerebellum.
evidence: Inferred from anatomical position and connectivity of UBCs.

claim: In the mouse cerebellum, Drd1 expressing UBCs reside in regions involved in processing vestibular signals and eye movements.
source: In the mouse cerebellum, Drd1 expressing UBCs reside in regions involved in processing vestibular signals and eye movements.
evidence: Observed from distribution of tdT+ UBCs in Drd1-Cre mice (Figure 1A) and known functions of these cerebellar regions.

claim: Drd1 receptors are expressed predominantly in ON UBCs.
source: Since we find that Drd1 receptors are expressed predominantly in ON UBCs, dopamine release from LC axons could coordinate with vestibular mossy fiber inputs to enhance signals arising directly from the semicircular canals (Balmer and Trussell, 2019).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunohistochemistry showing 71% of tdT+ UBCs express mGluR1 (Figure 1D), a marker of ON UBCs.

claim: Dopamine release from LC axons could coordinate with vestibular mossy fiber inputs to enhance signals arising directly from the semicircular canals.
source: Since we find that Drd1 receptors are expressed predominantly in ON UBCs, dopamine release from LC axons could coordinate with vestibular mossy fiber inputs to enhance signals arising directly from the semicircular canals (Balmer and Trussell, 2019).
evidence: Speculated based on current findings and prior literature (Balmer and Trussell, 2019).

claim: The recurrent subcircuit between Purkinje cells and UBCs has the potential to significantly regulate the output of the vestibulo-cerebellum.
source: Leveraging genetic access to a subpopulation of UBCs, we have characterized a new recurrent subcircuit between Pkj cells and UBCs, which has the potential to significantly regulate the output of the vestibulo-cerebellum.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing bidirectional connectivity between Pkj cells and UBCs (Figures 6-7).

claim: This work expands knowledge of cerebellar circuitry.
source: Altogether, this work expands our knowledge of cerebellar circuitry, resolves longstanding questions about the ability of TH+ Pkj cells to release dopamine, and points to the LC as the source of dopamine to the cerebellum.
evidence: Summary statement about the contributions of the current study.

claim: This work resolves longstanding questions about the ability of TH+ Purkinje cells to release dopamine.
source: Altogether, this work expands our knowledge of cerebellar circuitry, resolves longstanding questions about the ability of TH+ Pkj cells to release dopamine, and points to the LC as the source of dopamine to the cerebellum.
evidence: Demonstrated by FISH data showing TH+ Pkj cells lack machinery for dopamine synthesis and release (Figure 3D-F).

claim: This work points to the locus coeruleus as the source of dopamine to the cerebellum.
source: Altogether, this work expands our knowledge of cerebellar circuitry, resolves longstanding questions about the ability of TH+ Pkj cells to release dopamine, and points to the LC as the source of dopamine to the cerebellum.
evidence: Supported by anatomical tracing (Figures 3-4) and functional evidence from GRABDA2h imaging and electrophysiology (Figure 5).
